title: Medialunas
subtitle: Argentine sweet croissants glazed with honey syrup
excerpt: Soft, sweet, buttery croissants with a golden honey glaze, eaten for breakfast across Argentina. This recipe makes 12 medialunas and takes about 4 hours including proving time. They are sweeter and more pillowy than French croissants and are best eaten warm on the day they are baked.
sourceNotes: Medialunas, meaning half moons, are the Argentine version of the French croissant, introduced by French and Austrian immigrants in the late nineteenth century. They are sweeter and softer than French croissants, and are eaten at breakfast throughout Argentina, typically with a cortado coffee. Buenos Aires cafes are known for their fine medialunas.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled medialunas without the glaze. Reheat at 160C for 8 minutes and glaze while still warm.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made and laminated the night before. Refrigerate overnight after the final fold, then shape and prove in the morning.

content.text: This recipe makes 12 medialunas and takes about 4 hours from start to finish, most of which is resting time. The process has several stages and is best approached as a project for a free morning. Read the whole recipe before starting so you understand when the dough needs to rest and when it needs to be worked.

The lamination process, where you fold cold butter into the dough in repeated layers, is what creates the flaky layers. Keep the butter cold and work quickly so it does not melt into the dough. If at any point the dough becomes warm and greasy, wrap it and refrigerate for 20 minutes before continuing. The honey glaze is applied twice: once straight from the oven, once after 5 minutes, which builds up a glossy, sticky coating.

items.prepNote: cold and cubed for laminating, plus 30g softened for the dough
one for the dough, one beaten for glazing

content.text: Mix 7g fast-action yeast with 150ml warm milk and a pinch of sugar. Leave for 5 minutes until frothy. Combine with the flour, 60g sugar, 30g softened butter, 1 egg, 1 tsp salt and a few drops of vanilla extract. Knead for 8 minutes until smooth. Shape into a rectangle, wrap and refrigerate for 1 hour.
Place the 200g cold cubed butter between 2 sheets of baking paper and bash with a rolling pin into a flat rectangle roughly 15cm x 20cm. Keep it cold.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough into a rectangle roughly double the size of the butter block. Place the butter in the centre, fold the dough over it from both sides to enclose it completely, and press the edges to seal.

Roll the dough out into a long rectangle and fold it into thirds like a letter. Wrap and refrigerate for 30 minutes. Repeat this rolling and folding process 2 more times, chilling for 30 minutes between each fold.

After the final fold, roll the dough into a large rectangle about 4mm thick. Cut into triangles with a base of about 8cm. Roll each triangle from the base to the tip to form a croissant shape, curving the ends slightly. Place on lined baking trays.
Leave to prove at room temperature for 1 to 1.5 hours until puffed and almost doubled. Brush with beaten egg. Bake at 190C (170C fan) for 16 to 18 minutes until deep golden.

While they bake, warm 3 tbsp honey with 2 tbsp sugar and 2 tbsp water in a small pan until the sugar dissolves. Brush the medialunas twice with the warm honey glaze as soon as they come out of the oven. Serve warm.

attrs.symptom: No flaky layers, just a dense bread texture
attrs.cause: Butter melted into the dough during lamination instead of staying in separate layers
attrs.fix: Work in a cool kitchen and chill the dough for the full 30 minutes between each fold. If the dough looks greasy or the butter is seeping through, stop and refrigerate immediately.

attrs.symptom: Medialunas did not rise during proving
attrs.cause: Yeast was old or inactive, or the milk was too hot and killed it
attrs.fix: Test yeast by mixing it with warm (not hot) milk and a pinch of sugar. If it does not froth within 10 minutes, the yeast is dead and you need a fresh packet.

attrs.symptom: Medialunas are pale on the outside but doughy inside
attrs.cause: Oven temperature was too low, or they were underbaked
attrs.fix: They should be deep golden rather than pale gold. If the outside colours before the inside is cooked, reduce the temperature by 10 degrees and bake for 5 more minutes.

content.text: Buenos Aires is full of confiterias, old-fashioned cafes where medialunas are eaten at breakfast alongside a cortado or cafe con leche. The best ones are sticky with honey, soft in the middle and eaten warm from the basket. They are not a weekend treat in Argentina but a daily routine, the kind of breakfast people have on the way to work. Homemade ones, allowed to prove slowly and glazed properly, are a different thing from the supermarket version.
